author: Julius Gavroche
title: Giorgio Agamben: Political elections or opinion polls?
content:
Auguste Couder, 

Le Serment du Jeu de Paume, 20 juin 1789

. 1848







The fact that what we continue to call democracy has lost its meaning is demonstrated by the indiscriminate use of opinion polls, which lay bare the already obvious fact that elections are merely a survey of public opinion rather than an expression of political will. Opinion polls, by showing day by day—through fluctuations in respondents’ views—the numerical standing of the parties, carry out a sort of continuous election, which nobody controls and which can therefore, as indeed happens, be manipulated to in turn influence the very opinion it is supposed to reflect. We call democracy a government of public opinion; that is to say, of something politically entirely insubstantial, which has no reality other than the polls, which, at the very moment they appear to record it, create, alter and manipulate it incessantly. The process by which Rousseau’s 

volonté générale

 [general will]—which cannot be quantified—has gradually been transformed into public opinion, which is merely a matter of numbers, defines the fate of Western democracies.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: The Hot Potato Changes Hands Again
content:
On the 2026 Midterm Elections




from the 

CrimethInc. 

collective, 06/11/2026




Ultimately, the Democrats are no more capable of addressing the root causes of popular anger than the Republicans. State power will continue to swing back and forth more and more wildly between different parties until our rulers consolidate an autocracy or we manage to effect revolutionary change.










As we anticipated 

in April

, the death knell of the Trump era has rung. Despite being 

historically unpopular

, Democratic politicians won a sweeping victory in the November 2026 midterm elections. Many are describing the rout as an “

extinction-level event

” for the Republican Party.




All this should feel familiar. Only two years ago, when Democrats lost the 2024 elections, pundits across the political spectrum rushed to declare the collapse of the Democratic Party. Summarizing a widespread perception, one 

expert

 claimed that







“Fundamental shifts are occurring in the body politic that have left Democrats on the wrong side of the popular vote, congressional races, and the country’s shifting demographics.”







Two years later, people are saying the same things about the Republican Party. The backlash against Republicans in this year’s election eclipses the gains they made in 2024. Yet the pendulum has been swinging wildly back and forth between parties for over a decade now—and it could be that the wildest swings have yet to come.




For all the talk of political polarization, loyalty to political parties is at its 

lowest

 in decades. Since at least 2016, anger at the status quo has been the most powerful force in politics; Democrats like Hillary Clinton and Joe Biden who attempted to present themselves as its defenders have learned that the hard way. Likewise, Donald Trump has only able to win elections when he is not in office. Whenever Trump represents the ruling order, he draws the same backlash that he once managed to channel.




Since 2014, we have argued that state power itself has become a hot potato that burns whoever holds it. In a globalized economy, in which governments can no longer mitigate the impact of capitalism on their citizens without investors taking their money elsewhere, no party is able to hold state power for long without losing credibility with voters. Similarly, the challenges of maintaining position as a waning imperial power inevitably undercut the legitimacy of whoever controls the state: just as the genocide in Gaza damaged the Biden administration’s support, Trump’s 

war with Iran

 has contributed to driving away voters.




Similar things are taking place all around the world. 

British politicians

 have also seen rapid reversals in fortune. The centrist parties that have long ruled Germany and France are in precipitous decline. One Latin American government after another has swung to the far right, but that hardly indicates a 

social consensus

 in favor of 

any political camp

.




Only countries under continuous autocratic rule, such as Russia, Belarus, China, and North Korea, are excepted from the hot potato pattern. Donald Trump has made no secret of his desire to establish a similar state of affairs in the United States. Yet even in Hungary, which Republicans took as a model for their illiberal aspirations, the long-running autocratic government ultimately lost control. The same has occurred in Poland and, more recently, Serbia. Wherever voters have an opportunity—however narrow—to demand change, they do so—however arbitrarily and capriciously.




With no prospect of improving life for his rank-and-file supporters, Trump’s solution was to 

inflict violence

 on their behalf, offering them the vicarious thrill of watching the state cause harm to others as an outlet for their frustration. 

Less bread, more circuses

.




Republicans and Democrats—trash and recycling.




It might have worked—if ordinary people had not courageously taken the streets to interfere. We owe Trump’s failure to those who assembled at 

Tesla dealerships

 in spring 2025, who 

rose up

 against federal agents and the National Guard that June, who confronted Immigration and Customs Enforcement mercenaries in 

Chicago

, 

Minnesota

, and elsewhere. As we previously saw in 

the movement against police and white supremacy

, when people take risks in solidarity with others, this makes it possible for more people to experience empathy where previously, they only felt dissociation and apathy.




The grassroots resistance that emerged in response to the Trump administration stands in stark contrast to the way that elite figures across the political spectrum immediately put themselves as Trump’s disposal. Tech billionaires from Silicon Valley flocked to his inauguration to throw themselves at his feet. Powerful 

law firms

, university administrations, and 

corporations

 subordinated themselves to his will. Heads of state from across the world groveled and toadied to Trump—regardless of how he 

treated

 them, no matter how absurd his 

demands

.




Throughout 2025, Democratic politicians confined themselves to expressing opposition in purely symbolic ways, if occasionally 

at great length

. Cowardly centrist Democrats had already 

embraced Trump’s anti-immigrant politics

 well before the 2024 election; after it, many of them 

actively participated

 in the Trump regime’s attacks on immigrants, seizing the opportunity to call for the Democratic Party to continue tacking 

rightward

.




The scale of subsequent 

resistance

 to ICE showed that this was not hard-nosed pragmatism, but political opportunism at the service of xenophobia. A 

poll

 at the beginning of March 2026 showed that only 39% of respondents opposed abolishing ICE, with fully 50% actively calling for its abolition. The disparity between these figures and the very small number of politicians prepared to consider abolishing ICE even today shows that Democratic politicians will openly defy their supporters’ wishes in order to continue to advance a reactionary agenda. As politicians, they do not simply answer to a constituency of voters, but above all to a clientele of capitalists.




Trump did his best to rig the system in his favor ahead of the 2026 elections, arranging for widespread gerrymandering, seeking to control the voting process, and attempting to put the pieces in place to contest the results. Billionaires backed him financially—Elon Musk singlehandedly spent half a billion dollars, a quarter of the entire Republican budget for the election, in an effort to put his thumb on the scales. In the end, the results were so conclusive that none of this mattered. As in 2016, 2020, and 2024, the majority of voters rejected the reigning party.




Yet because this will was expressed via voting, rather than through more direct means, the result simply hands power to another coterie of politicians who will not address the needs of those who elected them. The more secure the Democrats’ grip on power becomes, the less they will concern themselves with the wishes of the electorate. If anything, the 2026 election will only embolden the centrists within the party, as it put power in the hands of more moderate Democrats, especially in swing districts.




But those who imagine that the Democrats did so well in the 2026 election on their own merits are fooling themselves.




The core issue at the root of the hot potato pattern is that the existing political order cannot address the instability, disparities, and crises of a capitalist system that has concentrated most of the wealth of society in the hands of a few while inflicting grievous social, psychological, and ecological damage on the rest of us. No political party will initiate the kind of revolutionary transformation that will be required to shift to a more egalitarian and sustainable way of life; such change can only come from grassroots mobilization. As long as there is no widespread, powerful social movement that offers the prospect of addressing these problems through profound change, people will continue rejecting one government after another in increasing desperation.




Silicon Valley tech moguls—who backed Joe Biden in 2020 only to switch sides in 2024—are even less popular than Donald Trump. Hatred of tech billionaires, data centers, and Flock cameras cuts across political lines; like the war on Iran, it is one of the factors that caused many former Trump voters to stay home or vote for Democrats. Yet as they regain their hold on power, Democrats will be inclined to work more and more closely with capitalists and the tech industry, rhetoric about “oligarchy” notwithstanding.







If social movements die down again as they did in 2021 after Biden took office, this will bode ill for the future, opening the way for even more extreme far-right reactionaries to pretend that they represent the only alternative to an unendurable status quo. If the 

cycle

 that played out between the first and second Trump administrations repeats itself again, the third iteration of far-right reaction will be more horrific than we can possibly imagine.




For good or ill, it does not look like anyone will be able to delude themselves into believing in a “return to normal” any time soon. The 

accession

 of Stephen Miller, an avowed white supremacist, to White House Chief of Staff sets the stage for the Trump administration to conclude with a period of brutal, open conflict. The administration lacks the support to win an open power struggle with the rest of society, but has left itself no alternative. As one 

New York Times

 commentator put it, “The next two years could actually be pretty volatile.”




As long as Trump remains in power, the far right will be perceived as the hegemonic force against which social anger will gravitate. But we must not wait for Democratic politicians to stand up to the Trump administration; even if they did, at best, that would function to relegitimize the same state institutions that will once again be turned against us in the future—as we saw in the Democrats’s response to the 

failed coup

 of January 6, 2021.




We must set an example by continuing to resist the Trump administration—and, wherever necessary, Democratic local and state administrations as well—through grassroots 

direct action

. Rather than simply waging a defensive struggle, we must figure out how to take proactive steps towards 

a completely different way of life

 in the process. Otherwise, the far right will eventually benefit once again from the inevitable disillusionment with Democratic administrations.




At best, the election results should function as a mandate for grassroots resistance to the Trump administration’s policies, not as a pressure valve for anxiety about them. We must build the grassroots capacity to defend and care for our communities. If we succeed, Democratic politicians will probably try to co-opt whatever we have achieved by offering to do the same things for us through the state. But they will only offer us what we demonstrate the ability to accomplish ourselves, and it is better to develop the ability to address needs directly and consistently than for the well-being of our communities to depend on the outcome of elections.




In short: it’s good to see Trump losing control. But the pendulum will continue to swing back and forth between political parties in wilder and wilder oscillations until we make revolutionary changes in our society.

content:
Woodcut by Frans Masereel







from Peter Gelderloos’ substack page, 

Suviving Leviathan

, 05/11/2026







Breathing Room




from the apocalyptic, fascistic Right to the insufficient, hypocritical, quietly genocidal Left




In the recent elections in Brasil, one of the largest countries in the Global South, leftwing darling Lula beat Flavio Bolsonaro, the fascistic dynast supported by the country’s plantation owner class. In Israel, the extreme Right lost the elections to the far Right (not a typo). And in the US, a “blue wave” has given the Democrats an ample margin of control in both chambers of Congress as well as a strong majority of governorships (for non-US readers, for whatever weird-ass reason related to our especially amnesiac, isolationist culture, in the US blue is the color of the Left and red is the color of the Right). In once Republican-held or toss-up states like Texas, North Carolina, and New Jersey, Democratic candidates won by double digits while conservatives won in what were, until yesterday, solidly Republican states like Florida or Louisiana by only 1 or 2%.







A high level Republican operative connected to Trump admitted to the press that these elections were just “too big to rig,” casually acknowledging how common it is to redraw electoral maps or send the precise vote-counting machines to the friendly districts and low quality, high-failure-rate machines to the unfriendly districts, in order to win an extra percentage point and tip elections.




Brasil




In Brasil, where former far Right president Jair Bolsonaro serves a sentence of house arrest in his mansion for launching a failed coup attempt after he lost the 2022 elections, his son Flavio Bolsonaro carried the first round of the elections in early October but failed to attain a majority. In the second round, held October 25

th

, voters turned to the Left and re-elected the incumbent, Lula, off the Workers’ Party. Wealthy investors punished the country for their vote, with the Brasilian stock market taking a plunge after the election even though Lula is a very business-friendly politician who has overseen a large deal of growth and “development” in the Brasilian economy. In practice that means he promotes oil drilling and mining in the Amazon, he subsidizes the intertwined beef-soy industry causing so much destruction in the south and west of the country, and he also supports manufacture and higher tech industry.







Brasil’s stock market index, with the big crash on the right-hand side occurring on October 25.







If Bolsonaro’s son Flavio had won this past 25

th

 of October, the death squads that work for the ranchers, soy plantation owners, miners, loggers, or directly for the state, would have had free rein. Several of my friends and many of the 

Indigenous

, 

African diasporic

, and lower class mestizo or white people 

I met last year

, people at the forefront of 

rural

 and 

urban struggles

 against the ongoing violence of colonial capitalism and 

for a better world

, would have been at greater risk of getting murdered for their resistance. For sure, a lot of people are breathing a very valid sigh of relief. But they’re not naïve about the meaning of the leftwing victory.




[Some of those links above go to 

Antimidia

 videos in Portuguese. Before pressing play, scroll down to “Legendas” and you’ll see buttons for English subtitles.]




As one friend put it, “

If Bolsonaro wins, they kill us; if Lula wins, they let us die.

” A second friend referred to a “mono-polarization” in which there are not two competing poles, just a single pole, “the extreme Right, which pulls everything into its proximity.”




Another friend described the following:







“Bolsonarismo already won. I don’t say that just because the Congress and Senate are controlled by fascists, I’m referring to Lula’s campaign replicating the methods of communication that are very close to fascism (including the name “Lula’s Army”). A few days ago on TV, Lula openly defended lowering the age at which children can be tried as adults (in order to appease the Right) and other similar things. Every time there is a “vote against fascism” which includes the attempt to also convince the Right or “center right,” the pendulum moves to the right.




“After the conservative reaction to 

the 2013 revolt

, some people (like the author Paulo Arantes) said that we were living in a situation with a horizon of diminishing expectations, without a view towards amplifying the struggles and the capacity to dream of a new world. It seems to me that now it’s worse: not only are they [the Left] slamming on the breaks, but the vital energy to struggle was channeled into the methods of the enemy.




“Perhaps what most calls my attention is how the argument for a “struggle for national sovereignty” was adopted in a terrible way. To combat Trump’s intervention pushing for a brutal extractivism to get so-called rare earth minerals, it is affirmed that [these lands and resources] are exclusively Brasilian, as though the problem were only who gets to destroy the Earth and not the destruction itself.”







And a fourth friend shared with a fair amount of alarm and heartbreak over how Lula’s campaign capitalized on the fear of Bolsonaro to break the sense of autonomy of a great many people in one of the strongest, most radical anticolonial and anticapitalist projects in the territories occupied by the Brasilian state. It even got so bad that some comrades accused those who refused to vote of secretly being Bolsonaro supporters.













This quote is from a message they sent me just before the election: “We’ll keep fighting, whoever wins. But here the possible re-election of Lula is referred to as a defeat of Bolsonarismo, and it’s nothing of the kind.”







They also recommended some texts, 

this one is an academic article

 in English, Portuguese, and Spanish about the People’s Web, an anticolonial “land back” network of communities based on direct action, mutual aid, and autonomy, and these two, which are in Spanish, address “

What Do They Mean When They Say Sovereignty?

” and “

Lands Without Borders, Owners, and Flags in Brasil and Argentina

.”







Friends, strangers, comrades, neighbors: we have been making this mistake for too fucking long. Literally millions of us have died in this struggle. We have to get smarter than binary thinking. 

If we can only consider two different options for our world, both of them are Death.

 Fuck antifascism, fuck anti-imperialism, and fuck the democrats, liberals, and Marxists who manipulate those concepts, if all they come to mean is that we have to support a slightly gentler form of colonialism, of white supremacy, of ecocide, of patriarchy. The slower path to Hell still takes you to Hell and, look around folks! We’ve arrived. False pragmatism and the extremely simple-minded strategy of “you have to vote for A because B is worse” have failed us catastrophically. Why on earth would we keep using a strategy that has brought us to this hellscape?




Other worlds are possible, they are already and still alive here in the cracks of the present system, and we desperately need to remember them, imagine them, believe in them, commit to them, and fight for them.




Israel




Let’s turn to the Israeli elections as a great example of the problem of supporting the lesser evil.




For Netanyahu and his colleagues, Arabic people voting in Israel is an existential “emergency.”




In Israel, 11 parties won seats in the Knesset. Nine of those parties are rightwing. The two leftwing parties won only 6% of the vote. And one of those parties (Democrats) isn’t even anti-genocide – they want to stop the ongoing wars and land theft but not necessarily to reverse the land theft and ethnic cleansing Israel is based on. The other, the Joint List, is led by Palestinians who have never been allowed to join the Israeli government. This was, truly, an election between the extreme Right and the far Right. The Opposition coalition won 48 seats in the Knesset, 40 of which are divided amongst three rightwing parties, and 8 of which belong to the only Israeli leftwing party. (Yep! That means that of the Israeli [non-Arabic] part of the electorate, less than 8% vote for the Left, and the rest vote for the far Right or extreme Right.)




The primary campaign promise of the Opposition coalition, led by Gadi Eisenkot’s Yasher party, was to remove Netanyahu from power, not because of all his wars and genocide, but because he’s not doing a great job at those wars and genocide. Polling consistently shows that 

the vast majority of Israelis

 are 

in favor of the genocide

 and 

the wars against Lebanon, Syria, and Iran

, but majorities were 

upset with Netanyahu

 that his government did not 

win the release of the prisoners held by Hamas

 quickly enough and that the methods being used by West Bank settlers 

might lead to more sanctions

 and a loss of support from “the international community” (Europe and the US). Also, many are miffed that *Haredi or Ultra-Orthodox Jews have 

historically been exempted

 from obligatory military service; they want all Israeli citizens to participate in the military. Others are upset with the fact that Netanyahu is avoiding a prison sentence by staying in office. He got convicted, not for war crimes, but for a pretty clear case of corruption.




*(Haredi make up a significant number of the 800,000 settlers living illegally—but with the full support of the state—in the West Bank and East Jerusalem on recently stolen land, and the political parties representing them are a part of Netanyahu’s coalition. To be clear, the Ultra-Orthodox are often the vanguard of the genocide as they attack, burn, plunder, and murder in the West Bank, they just don’t put on a uniform to do it. 

The number of West Bank settlers has roughly doubled in the last 20 years

.)




The second major promise made by the Opposition was to maintain the official, white supremacist tradition in Israeli politics and not to let any Arabic-led party into the government. Since Netanyahu’s party, Likud, still got the most votes (though they lost 9 seats in the Knesset and their ultra-nationalist allies lost a cumulative 5 seats), the only way for the Opposition to keep both of those promises is to rule with a minority coalition that does not include the two Palestinian-led parties but relies on their votes for investiture and critical legislation, which means a really solid practice of compromise. That shouldn’t be so difficult. Both of those parties have said they would do whatever it takes to get rid of Netanyahu and stop some of the more extreme new settlement projects in the West Bank.




That shouldn’t be too hard a compromise. After all, the rightwing Opposition wants to get rid of Netanyahu, and they’re okay with stopping some settlement projects since those empower their political competitors in the Orthodox camp and could hurt their economy by leading to more sanctions. The only thing that could stop them from winning control of the government is their own racism. So… I give them a 50/50 shot, at best. 

Recent polls support that kind of pessimism.

: incredibly few Israelis believe any land should be given back to the Palestinians* or that recently built settlements should be dismantled. They don’t believe the settlements are wrong, but 50% said the policy of land theft and construction in the West Bank should be “adjusted to avoid sanctions escalation and international isolation”. Amongst Netanyahu’s bloc, however, a solid majority said “the government should continue the policy ‘whatever the price’.” 52% of those polled said they could accept sanctions on individual settlers who were especially violent, but 63% opposed international sanctions being placed on goods coming from illegal settlements (“illegal,” in the media, referring to Palestinian lands stolen since the Oslo accords of 1993, not all the land stolen before that). With very few exceptions, most Israelis only oppose the daily violence of settlers in the West Bank if it might hurt them personally. As 

The Guardian

 put it: “The poll suggests that the more people feel they will be damaged personally, the more they oppose the settlement policy.”




[*Some Israeli politicians do support giving desert lands, much of it the traditional territory of Bedouins, to Palestinians as a non-consensual exchange to permanently take over more fertile Palestinian lands.]







The bullet and the ballot to keep Palestinians down. Invaders vote at an official polling station set up in the West Bank.







Here’s more detail from other polls. 

In May 2024

, after 7 months of the war on Gaza, only 4% of Israelis thought the country’s assault had gone too far, half thought Israel should directly govern Gaza after the war, and only 8% thought that the people of Gaza should be allowed to choose their own government. By that point, 

Israel had directly killed over 35,000 Palestinians in Gaza

, not counting increased deaths from disease or hunger, they had seriously injured 80,000, and forced 1.7 million out of their homes – completely destroying most of the homes along with all the belongings in them. Over 90% of Israelis thought that was the right thing to do. Actually, that’s incorrect. Half the Israelis polled thought the genocide “had not gone far enough”.




Another year of genocide didn’t soften that view. In August 2025, a poll carried out by an Israeli organization found that 76% of Israelis believed that “

there are no innocents in Gaza

,” tacitly approving of the mass murder of children and noncombatants. The poll was conducted “amid rising racist attacks against Palestinians in occupied territories and Palestinian citizens of Israel.”




An August 2026 poll found that the Israeli public supported the wars against Iran, Lebanon, and Syria, but were “

dissatisfied with the results

,” namely the failure to achieve regime-change in Iran and the slowdowns (so-called ceasefires that the Israeli military violates multiple times every day) in the invasions of Lebanon and Syria. A March 2026 poll published by the 

Times of Israel

 found that 

78% of Israelis supported the war against Iran

 (which at that point had killed at least 1,500 Iranian civilians and an unknown number of Iranian soldiers). Even half of Israelis who identified themselves as leftwing supported the war.







Actually, this isn’t Lebanon, it’s “Greater Israel.”







In conclusion, elections, democracy, and the Left won’t stop Israel’s genocide and ongoing wars because:







the vast majority of Israelis are pro-genocide




even the Left is pro-genocide and half of the Left is pro-war




the Israeli leftwing party only got 6% of the vote, which was a huge gain for them.

The US




The sweeping victory of the Democrats in yesterday’s election illustrates a point I was trying to make in “

The Right’s Rollercoaster to Hell

.” By huffing the fumes of their own ideology of power too deeply, by zealously attacking anyone they perceive as a threat to the established order, the Right frequently damage the basis of their own power. And, at least in the anglosphere, the Right have not had intelligent strategists since the days of Margaret Thatcher and Henry Kissinger. Since then, they’ve just been getting dumber and dumber.




Many people have gotten furious with the rightwing attacks: people who need abortions, people who need access to healthcare, trans folks who want to be treated like people, Black folks who need an end to centuries of lynching, exclusion, and exploitation, Muslims sick of being portrayed as terrorists and invaders, latinas and African immigrants who were being attacked regardless of their status, and all the people who don’t belong to those groups but have loved ones who are, or all those who oppose bigotry and oppression on principle. (Basically, all those whom moderate Democrats refer to as fringe groups or the “woke.”




Then there’s the fact that the stupidity of the Trump regime was wrecking the US economy. While the billionaires keep raking it in, the dollar has lost about 9% of the value it had at the beginning of 2024, 

real wages have been stagnating or falling

, 

underemployment is high

, 

groceries have been getting more expensive

, 

food insecurity, electricity, and gas prices are all going up

, 

rent has increased 44% since 2019

 and 

mortgage rates are almost three times as high

 as they were in 2021. Obviously, all those things are much harder on working class and lower income people, while the rich don’t even notice the price of gas and groceries.




So again, it’s no surprise that most people wanted a big change. This map, showing how far to the left or right the vote went compared with 2024, is a pretty clear illustration.







Three short red arrows showing the districts that shifted a little to the right. Hundreds of long blue arrows showing all the districts that moved far to the left.










Incidentally, the US stock market

 surged 

after the leftwing victory. Remember how the opposite occurred in Brasil? The market has no

 invisible hand

, and there’s no cutthroat, mercenary competition intrinsic to human nature. It’s evil rich fuckers who want Brasil to maintain itself as a plantation for the global economy, where the millionaire landowners and mine owners can easily pay cops or paramilitaries to murder labor organizers or Indigenous people who might get in the way of their investments. The very same banks, corporate execs, and multimillionaire or billionaire investors want the US to maintain a more complex economy with a huge market to import goods from around the world alongside a well educated class of researchers who can be subsidized to develop pharmaceutical, chemical, alternative energy, and computing technologies that will result in trillions of dollars of profits. But a poorer population and major cuts to research subsidies can’t sustain that kind of economy. Clearly, the State is more powerful than capitalists on their own and the capitalists don’t always get their first choice, but they’ll make do with their second. They’ll profit in Brasil under Lula, and they’re happy that things in the US are turning around but if the most powerful government in the world goes too far Left or too far Right or just too far stupid, the capitalists will take their investments elsewhere and a new coalition of powerful states will arise to uphold the global order once NATO can’t hack it. They’re already in the wings, preparing. But maybe there’s another sort of change that could happen…







With a solid majority in Congress, the Democrats will get the opportunity to pass a budget next year that they could use to defund ICE, end military aid to Israel, and restore money to public education, scientific research, and social services related to healthcare, food poverty, and support for disabled people. They can also investigate corruption in the Trump administration, ICE conspiracies to murder or otherwise violate the rights of immigrants and rapid response people, and other instances of law breaking by government officials. And if they don’t fuck it up, they’ll probably win the presidency and keep a congressional majority in 2028.




What’s more, 

progressive candidates swept a number of elections

, including in toss-up states and districts, disproving the rhetoric of the Party establishment that more voters will support moderates and leftwing candidates can’t win competitive elections. That means there’s a possibility for the party as a whole to support more progressive policies by 2028, though of course the 

New York Times

 is scrounging for any statistical manipulation or talking head or can claim the elections were a vindication of the moderate Democrats, CNN is offering AIPAC a free platform to spread Islamophobia and reinforce the idea that responsible politicians have to support Israel’s genocide, and every person or institution with power and money to the left of Hitler is trying to reinforce the idea that Jeffries and Schumer are the best possible leaders of the Party, in the hopes of preserving a pro-police, pro-deportation, pro-billionaire, pro-AI, pro-Israel agenda.




So what do all these results mean for some important questions? What kinds of changes might we expect from the electoral victories of the Left?




—




Possible







The most recent right-wing wave that has seen governments across the Americas, Europe, Africa, and Asia shift to the Right may break, at least for now.










More marginalized and lower class populations will probably get access to government-funded resources.




Some workplace protections, environmental regulations, and rights to healthcare will be expanded or restored.




The repression against anticolonial and anticapitalist movements might shift to softer tactics.




The war against Iran might end, for now.







As a low-income person who relies on government assistance for healthcare, with a lethal (but fortunately very slow-moving) cancer caused by environmental toxins, who generally works jobs that involve dangerous or unhealthy conditions and few to no benefits, and who participates in movements constantly subjected to surveillance and repression, and with beloved friends who experience more brutal forms of repression that I don’t, I’m happy for all of these things. They make a difference. But is that difference enough?




—




Not Gonna Happen







We won’t be freed of the obligation to work for bosses in jobs that are often humiliating, unhealthy, and unsafe.




Poverty won’t disappear.




We won’t be allowed to have an unalienated relationship with our homes and the land: housing will continue to be designed as a way to enrich the wealthy and preserve our dependence on them, and land will continue to be treated as property.




Prisons and police won’t disappear, and the routine torture and brutality they produce will continue.




Political repression of anarchists, autonomous movements, and Indigenous communities fighting to get their land back won’t end, and when the Left is in power those facing repression will receive less solidarity and more isolation.




No historical form of oppression like white supremacy or patriarchy will disappear; they will continue to operate through and intensify systemic features like work, poverty, housing, policing, and repression.




Israel will not stop the genocide against Palestinians.




Indigenous peoples around the world will not be allowed to have autonomy over their land and culture.




Governments and corporations from Europe, North America, and South and East Asia will not stop sponsoring wars, genocide, slave labor, and deadly mining and plantation industries across sub-Saharan Africa.




Greenhouse gas emissions reductions will not happen fast enough to avert the acceleration of the worst mass death and mass extinction events in human history. Many years, there will be no emissions reductions at all.




Real emissions reductions, when they do occur, will be based on energy technologies that prioritize economic growth and cause a huge boom in land theft, toxic mining, death squads, and habitat destruction.




Other forms of ecocide and extractivism like industrial agriculture will continue to kill the soil, destroy the forests and wetlands, abuse workers, brutalize hundreds of millions of non-human animals, and drive ongoing land theft and genocide against Indigenous peoples.




The list only continues…







These elections have won us a little bit of breathing room, nothing more. The only way to create the kinds of change we need for survival is through waves of revolution that destroy, abolish, transform, and heal all the vestiges of that trinity of evil – capitalism, colonialism, and the State.




Those three forces are inseparable. They can’t be reformed, and none of them can be abolished while leaving the others intact. Only the State has ever existed without the other two but the emergence of colonial capitalism transformed all the various state models in the world into the modern state, which has proven unable to abolish capitalism no matter how many red flags it waves.




We have an extremely low chance of helping to launch these waves of revolution, sticking to it, adapting, overcoming, and winning, and if we do succeed it’s a labor that requires generations. And yet, it’s a bet we need to take, because there’s a 100% chance of immense suffering and death under the present system. There’s a 0% chance of reforming this system into something good through the methods of change it offers us, like elections. And, of the dozens of authoritarian Left revolutions that have succeeded in their strategy of seizing state power, exactly 0 have abolished capitalism, oppressive hierarchies, poverty, wars, or ecocidal ways of living.




How about we give a chance to the methods and traditions of struggle that have always predicted that would be the outcome of electoral reform or revolutionary states? How about we give a chance to the methods and traditions of struggle that have always rejected colonial society and fought for a world of 

ecocentric communities

 organized through 

rooted networks

 and mutual aid?

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Giorgio Agamben: Neolithic conservative
content:
Paul Goodman, one of the most radical anarchist thinkers of the twentieth century, once described himself as a “Neolithic conservative”. And Ivan Illich, who believed he had one foot in the Catholic tradition and the other in the mire of his own time, said that his orthodoxy was so ancient and complete as to be revolutionary. This means that to understand and perhaps even to undo the historical era in which we live, we must keep one foot in prehistory. This situation on the threshold or at the boundary between two incommensurable eras is precisely what our age proves incapable of. Not only does it think in a single dimension, but it has lost all connection with its own past, without which any access to the present is impossible. For this reason, it can only look towards a future which, in reality, is nothing but the consequence of a past of which it is totally unaware, and which pulls its strings like a marionette. Only those who stand on two legs between the past and the present can come to terms with both and not be unconsciously determined by them. Only a Neolithic conservative can be revolutionary enough to open up a new space for thought and action.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: To demonstrate
content:
from 

paris-luttes

, 02/11/2026







Yes, there are many of me within me. I take my feet in both hands, I put my shoes on. I check my armour, my gear. T-shirt, shorts, water bottle. I set off on the assault. I am someone else, thus armed. My head, my body—I’m going to rid them of the world’s grime.







I pound the tarmac, I pound the cobblestones, I stride through the city to write with my feet: I am here. I run, I watch the city pass by, I slip away from it, I leave it behind. Here we are, partners; I do not endure it, I look it in the eye and I see: its eyes answer me. Rise up! I am not who they want me to be. I am who I am, and I see the signs of the people just like me.




The people have marched, have walked the city just as I have. The most combative among them were chased by the police. They are young; they, too, are fit and healthy. The robotic men, the tools of those who want us to be as they want us to be, those very ones—those helmeted robots, heavily armoured and armed—charged at them, assaulted them, tear-gassed them, or even maimed them, or even rounded them up, or even imprisoned them, or even killed them. But they—armed, like me, with nothing but their trainers, armed with lightness—even when suffocated, even when wounded, even when maimed, even when locked away, even when dead—they remained free. And our freedom will outlive us. What history will remember is our freedom, our honour. And the injustice, the dishonour of those who have used their wretched power—their usurped power—to destroy our homes, our country, the way we live in our country, and to send their robots to stifle our voices.




My voice is silenced, but our feet remain. I stride through the city and hear the shattering of glass spewed from the bins that the people’s anger has overturned. I run; my run is a fire that lifts and purifies my anger. You shall not have us, you shall not have me, says my path. I thank the people who are rising up, just as with every stride my old body rises up and regains its youth.




I run amongst the rubble. The old world crumbles beneath my wind-swept soles. Our rulers look askance, they who cannot even govern themselves. Drugs circulate in the circles where they shut themselves away, they whose minds are occupied only with the endless repetition of the same. This is the time of tyrants, tyrants to be deposed. The demon Money reigns over humans, stray animals abandoned by the wisdom of the Earth. It has taken possession of cohorts of souls, bending them so thoroughly to its will that they can no longer even tell day from night. Illegitimate in the eyes of Life, they have spawned the fallen spirits of tyranny, pawns who have become parasites upon the entire planet.




Keep running, planet! I run with you and I love you. See, streams flow through me, breezes caress me; I was born to run, not to die! From my muscles spring forth greenery, beasts, stars. For as I run, I walk with all living things that tread the earth; I walk against the walls of the circles within which the rulers and their lackeys alienate themselves. The makers of artificial books are alarmed by the artificial intelligence that ridicules them, and I laugh—yes, long live technology! I belong to the world that marches on. May it wipe out the forgers and bloodsuckers, the white-collar cannibals, the show-offs who unbutton their shirts to reveal their meagre chests, the non-living beings thirsty for glory and money.




Our home is our country, our country is the world, and these people are driving us out of it. Just as Paris was besieged during the Games, with barriers everywhere, police everywhere, the army everywhere, public spaces seized, movement restricted, running or walking amounting to navigating a maze like in those children’s magazines where you have to search for and trace a path with a pencil to the exit, this is what cities have become in their darkest form when the people demonstrate there and one must escape the traps, escape police violence, escape the bans on gathering or moving here or there, and then the ban on demonstrating in city centres, with those in power behaving as if the country belonged to them, our country, our home, for every country belongs to those who live in it; a ban on living in it, with those in power behaving like colonisers towards their own people because, in their eyes, we are the ones who are nothing, whilst they, for their part, are among those who have succeeded – succeeded in selling off the country, succeeded in destroying the country, succeeded in seizing the country to hand it over to all the mine exploiters, of our country, this goldmine that those in power have handed over to them to ravage; listen to me, I am running, I am panting, my old body rises up just as the people rise up, and we rediscover our youth; I rediscover the youth of my country, free and inventive, inventing their lives despite the contempt shown towards them by so many of their country’s elders, the future of this country despite the arrogance, despite the deafness, despite the blindness of so many who sit idly in this country, so many who have grown stale—of whom I might well be one were it not for my running, were it not for my defiance, with my feet and my body, against the labyrinths of power.




The insurgents are queens and kings, standing tall on their own two feet. The method? One step at a time. They march, they erect barricades, they entrench themselves and find other ways through. Thus the spring: torrential at first, then widening its course until it reaches its estuary. I run, I walk, I see the people rising up, moving forward; I feel like crying. Because it is within me that the surging crowd rises up, it is in my flesh that the torrent wells up and seeks to overflow—through my throat, through my eyes—I, a poor creature swept away by the joyful pain of unity.




Whoever walks through the city manifests the life that springs from cosmic accidents. Stand up, you wretch; it is time to tear yourself free from the traps that bind your ankles; now it is through the body that one must dream! But go forth wisely; do not let them sacrifice you or ruin you on their stinking altar; go forth with resolve—wisdom and resolve will prevail, and I see that you possess them; I admire that you do. It is through the body that we must go to inhabit the home they deprive us of: our city, our country, our planet. The streets are ours, and so is the countryside. To hell with the ministries; we belong to the earth—our dead are our roots, from which we draw our strength; our generations, who have taken the names of letters, are our fruits and must return to the beginning. I run; my heart pounds against the cobblestones; my cheeks are red; and I breathe the epic breath of revolutions. The living surge through my muscles, the peoples surge through my voice; it is not I who run, it is not I who speak—I am but a vessel, a vessel carrying art into animality, a surge of forms and colours in fur and plumage! Let us ascend to bliss.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Halloween riots as youth uprising pushes on
content:
Photograph: Alain Jocard/AFP







from 

Freedom News

, 2 November 2026







Against efforts by systemic forces to keep youth discontent in check, decentralised insurrection and autonomy continue to break through




Blade Runner




Halloween weekend saw mass protests throughout 

France

, 

Albania

, 

Germany

, 

Switzerland

 and 

Portugal

, with riots erupting across multiple cities.







As Gen Z–led insurrections flare up globally, a neo-fascist surge has risen steadily alongside them. In the UK, the 

assault on Freedom Bookshop

 sounds a clear warning and a reminder that the street-level provocations escalating across the country over the past few years are happening for a reason.




Systemic actors seek to keep the 

youth’s insurgent tendencies

 in check, deliberately redirecting anger toward vulnerable groups such as 

migrants

. This manufactured resentment is predictable amid ever-increasing housing and living costs for the working classes, pushing an increasing number of people to the margins.




At a time when Western superpowers engage in proxy wars and genocides abroad while leading an arms race at home, they ask their citizens to live with less and prepare for disaster.




This dynamic stems directly from the neoliberal restructuring of Western production in the 1980s. Designed to crush the advances of previous labour movements, it enforced the TINA (“There Is No Alternative”) dogma across politics and culture alike. Consequently, it has become increasingly difficult to imagine alternative ways of surviving, let alone navigating complex issues like personal liberty, identity, equality, and disagreement.




What mainstream news decries as a “shocking” resurgence of patriarchal misogyny among young people is often just youth mimicking adult behaviour—mirroring the brutality of genocidal wars and the competitive ethos of streaming media. Reproduced in schools and everyday life, hegemonic neoliberal ethics instil a worldview based on survival of the fittest, top-dog dominance, and “kill or be killed.”




Yet what this apparatus of indoctrination tries to suppress is the simple fact that when left to their own devices, most people naturally build networks of communal solidarity and mutual aid. In Serbia, following the Novi Sad canopy collapse and subsequent police violence, 

student movements organised

 their resistance through confederated horizontal councils, effectively shifting the national political narrative. When elections arrived, they took the difficult decision to form an independent list that won national elections on 25 October 2026, ousting the Vu?i? regime after 15 years in power.




Representative democracy may not be a vehicle for social revolution, but this effort demonstrates the power of prefigurative politics. It proves that young people can mock authority, circumvent top-down structures, and channel the rage generated by class war into creative, radical action.




Where horizontal councils represent 

organised prefigurative power

, the unguided unruliness of marginalised youth represents its raw, volatile foundation. Neofascist networks, nurtured by neoliberal centres, actively attempt to capture this untapped energy—redirecting class anger away from the ruling class to protect existing power structures. Yet as Gen Z leads insurrections worldwide, state attempts to enforce “law and order” inevitably generate contested spaces of disorder.




Radical left and anarchist currents meet the youth in these spaces, where bands of poor kids raised in the hinterlands of 21st-century capitalism disrupt the peace of petty bourgeois business owners. Their unguided discontent with the commodity society is a crude but authentic attempt to claim back autonomy. When survival is squeezed down to petty crime and syndicate work, roaming the streets at night with loot in hand becomes simultaneously alienating and liberating—an experiential truth of street-level autonomy that no top-down political theory can fully capture.




This reality explains the state’s aggressive attempts to criminalise and persecute horizontal protest structures, such as 

Palestine Action in the UK

, which has not only struck major blows against domestic arms supply chains but has inspired offshoots across Europe and the US. The state relies on an old tactic: conflating separate legal cases to try activists together as members of an organised crime enterprise. The goal is to prevent the generalisation of dissent.




The group 

Rouvikonas

, who in Greece have also been targeted in this way, noted in a recent statement: “The symbolic weight of our actions strips political capital from the top and transfers it down to the grassroots of society. And when our actions go beyond symbolism and secure small victories, we are no longer just talking about political capital, but a threat by example.”




No matter how hard the efforts to divide insurgents between “good protesters” and “bad rioters,” it has once again proven difficult to prevent the 

struggle within the struggle

 from emerging—a tension “between the ‘protest-revindication-reform’ tendency linked to the left, and a more autonomous, more aggressive tendency that proposes a direct attack on State institutions and commodities.”




Feelings of anger cannot be buried; social rage drives a diverse body of people to the streets to express their discontent through varied means, 

uniting their voices

 to demand an end to systemic oppression. The current wave of revolts reminds us that the state, its fascist proxies, and the political establishment can only keep people feeling helpless temporarily. Against every attempt by state and capital to capture insurrection, life finds a way to break through the paved floor—revealing the beautiful chaos of decentralised communal organisation among free living beings.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Giorgio Agamben: The countless people
content:
One of the fundamental political problems — if not the most urgent — is how to conceive of an uncountable multiplicity (or multitude). As a political concept, the people only makes sense on condition that it is uncountable; if it can be counted, then what is decisive is no longer the people as such, but a numerical quantity — the so-called majority — into which the people dissolves according to the perverse mechanism of elections or plebiscites. The people—like the human race—are not a collection of countable singularities: the “popular” or “generic” character—that is to say, the political character—must belong entirely to the singular as such. This is what Marx sought to articulate through the concept of 

Gattungswesen

 (“generic being”), which defines each individual and not a countable quantity. Insofar as each individual “refers to himself as the present and living genus”, the people cannot be a numerical sum of individuals, but is an essential reality fully present in each one. Leviathan

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Intifada and fascism. Resisting humans, affirming monsters
content:
by Rodrigo Karmy Bolton




from 

Ficción de la razón

, 27/10/2026







It has become fashionable, thanks to sociological bureaucracy, to claim that the danger of any uprising is that it leads to fascism. That fascism can capitalise on it, turn it into an electoral and political enterprise, and triumph by harnessing its power and transforming it into a force. They used to say that revolt expresses “anomie” – that is, a normative mismatch with social dynamics – and that it was “violent” and “senseless” in that it involved burning things, looting shops and disrupting the “normal” flow of events. Now they say it leads to fascism and that, for that reason, it must be avoided at all costs. That if Le Pen wins at the French polls, it will have been due to the undeniable revolt; for if 

Kast

 won in Chile, his victory would have been due precisely to that. The revolt would be anomic, violent and, moreover, reactionary. Nothing could be more of a threat to progressivism than the people taking to the streets; nothing could torment its pedagogical mindset more than a crowd on a war footing.







But there are certain things here—too long-standing, too antiquated—which, nevertheless, must be recalled: first and foremost, the argument that revolt leads to fascism (however complex it may be) obscures the question of why fascism exists, why it arose, if not from decades of violent neoliberal reforms which have literally left people on the streets, landless, 

with no place in the world

. How are we to interpret the case of 87-year-old 

Maricarmen

, who was evicted from the house she was renting because she could not pay the rent? Evicted from their homes and left out in the open, the people today are all Palestinians; they are all Maricarmen: they live landless, homeless, with a longing to return. Neoliberal reforms that have been imposed across the globe and which have now entered a new phase in their process of intensification, where they have had to resort to “so-called primitive accumulation” to escape the stagnation that their own model – their own “civilisation” – has produced.




In its various forms, neo-fascism—steeped in melancholic passions and capitalising on public panic—has been the means by which the model has chosen to realise itself, accelerating its processes of accumulation. To this end, it needs to bury any form of state-legal framework capable of curbing or containing its momentum, thereby hastening the fulfilment of a sort of “

parousia

” of capital in which, at last, capital encounters no restraints whatsoever and is definitively consolidated upon the earth. A new process of plunder, dispossession and conquest of the earth has begun to consolidate the new machine of death: the artificial intelligence corporations that have made war the leap through which they seek to break free from their own stagnation. Led by the super-rich, the violent process of acceleration through which they set out to appropriate new lands is meeting with resistance.




The global intifada—which is nothing other than a field of multiple interdependencies—becomes the disruption of worlds rising up against the levelling imposed by capital. Whilst the latter strips peoples of their lands, their landscapes and their places, the intifadas disrupt this levelling to reweave interdependencies between worlds precisely where capital and its globalisation seek to triumph: without distance, without fissures, without chasms—merely bodies pressed together. Capitalism reveals itself today in a completely transparent manner. There is no need to dream of a “behind-the-scenes” force manipulating history; it is enough to experience what happens every day: psychological disasters, the proliferation of genocides, the frantic efforts to work in the informal sector, widespread precariousness, and the systematic exclusion from our cultural, social and political rights. The repeated discourses of the old fogies who thought they were lecturing us after the October uprising—claiming that the uprising was lawless, violent and, moreover, that it would lead to fascism—believed themselves to be effective, but strictly speaking, they have been nothing but empty words, like all pedagogy today.




Young people have taken to the streets. Uninterrupted, for years now: today in France, Spain and Albania; previously in Chile, Iraq and the United States. The old fogies tell young people that they are “apolitical”, that they admire Spider-Man rather than Lenin, and they resort to the same old rhetoric about order: what applies to the uprising applies to “young people” – lawless, violent and, ultimately, “fascists”. Young people, too, are supposedly “fascists”. Not only should they go to the psychiatrist to manage their ADHD, depression or panic attacks, but they should also listen to the old fogies so they can lecture them on what democracy is and why it should be respected. And then comes the “left”: who really cares about that discussion at the very moment of our mass murder? Who could possibly care when it comes to the destruction of our life force? The bureaucrats will be satisfied, but always unhappy. For they believe that unhappiness is the norm. The sheer scale of the intifadas, their spill over at regional and global levels – spill over which, in turn, has been channelled into mapping new flows of insurrection across the globe, flows that remain invisible to the canons of representation – has flooded the Earth and has continued to do so for some time now. The intifadas lay bare the transparent corruption of public power, the war inherent in private power, the ecological disaster into which we have been plunged, and the massive devastation that has become an everyday reality.




Well, it is not the intifadas that lead to fascism. It is the violence of the state-capital, implemented over decades of neoliberalism, that underpins its stage and provides its space. The super-rich are its director; the apparatus of control and security, its stage. The intifada becomes their threat, the monstrosity that looms before the upright “humans” who besiege and devour the masses. For it is not a question of establishing a “civilisation” to make us “human”; rather, it is that the “humans” have waged an endless war against any form of life that transcends their models. The Palestinians, the poor, the migrants 

are not human

. They become monsters. And this is precisely the war between humans and monsters. We – like every living being – are nothing more than monsters inhabiting the interface between worlds. For centuries, the “humans” have sought to assert their dominance over the monsters. And when they have wiped them out, they have annihilated themselves. Our happiness on earth lies in inhabiting our monstrosity, travelling ceaselessly between worlds; and so, like 

Gabriela Mistral

 in “

Poem of Chile

“, we sing of the journey, we sing of our inhabiting the interface—that place no satellite can locate, yet which smoulders within us like the eternal fire through which the voices of the dead never cease to mingle with those of the living.




The bureaucrats will try to convince us – yet again – that life is meant for ruling and not for inhabiting; that play is useless, that stupidity serves only the master and the boors who accompany him, and that “success” and “profit” are the only things that matter. The literature of our bodies is good for nothing more than being sanitised by the “experts” in monsters, those who, at the slightest hesitation, declare us terrorists. That is what is at stake in the European uprisings, because it is what has been at stake in the various uprisings that have erupted over recent decades: not a programme, not a political project, not an electoral machine, but something far less significant yet perhaps far more threatening: a vital passion that yearns desperately to inhabit, a literature of bodies intertwined at the interface of worlds. A literature of monsters, the misfits who belong nowhere, who have been cast out for being too old, perhaps ugly, for being useless or simply for being poor. The intifada is against the “humans”, now that they have cloaked themselves in Zionism, now that, once again, they believe themselves to be “chosen” to occupy the Earth.




In any case, the plan is clear: just as in Palestine, to expel us, annihilate us, lock us away. Fascism only comes about thanks to the bureaucrats who concoct the fiction that revolt leads to fascism, thanks to that left which wants nothing to do with insurrection, which turns a blind eye to street violence, thereby leaving the dirty work to the police. Returning to the Earth means populating the interworlds, at the interface where they intersect, in the resonances that each carries of the other, where each is a mixture and their plurality is variegated rather than individualised. Fascism is not merely a friend of bureaucracy but rather 

bureaucracy itself, at its most efficient

, whose ultimate form crystallises in AI and its imperialist corporations.




Nothing can renew our spirits without embracing our monstrosity: the interregnum is our place, monstrosity our way of existing on Earth. If “humans” – monsters devoid of affection, devoid of eroticism—have denied their monstrous condition by repeating “resentment” as the condition by which they tame their passions to play a part in a highly technological machine of mass murder, precisely so as not to be “affected” by the very efficiency of the task they carry out, we must affirm it: we are the monsters who declare war on the “humans” and their arrogant civilisation. Neither animals nor humans. Monsters: creatures of the interface who dance amongst the multiplicity of worlds and their interdependencies.




October 2026

author: Julius Gavroche
title: October 17th, or the Return of Playfulness
content:
from 

lundimatin

 #539, 26/10/2026







“Opportunistic delinquency,” “holiday-strike,” “lack of political maturity,” “childish cosplay,” “reckless destruction,” “acts of rage” — all these hostile terms used to discredit the ongoing uprising have given rise to their political antonyms: “material reappropriation,” “demands for better study conditions,” “political awareness,” “joyful staging,” and so on. October 17th has been the occasion for a prolific and all-encompassing production of a staggering number of counter-interpretations, theoretical texts, and hypotheses about what drives the movement. Yet, a subterranean dimension to its actions, omnipresent throughout, still seems to be ignored: playfulness [

le ludique

]. Without returning to a thorough examination of the underlying causes of the movement, nor to a prescriptive reading of its aftermath—most often guided by the intention to “manage” the movement—we wanted here to recapture the passion at work behind the riotous gestures and the high school fervour.




“Je te tiens, tu me tiens, par la barbichette, le premier de nous deux qui rira aura une tapette!”

[“I hold you, you hold me, by the goatee, the first one to laugh will get a light slap!”)

[1]




The Game Begins




Our hypothesis, which can coexist with others, posits that the “playful” comes into play as a uniquely effective concept for understanding the fundamentally joyful riotous activity around which the subjectivities of those participating in the insurrection were emotionally bound and organised.







Whether in the charivaris, carnivals, or parades of high school students dressed as comic book superheroes, the fact remains: play coupled with laughter constitutes an undeniable domain of tactics and stratagems allowing one to temporarily break free from the grip of a dominant power. But this playful aspect is neither a simple formal reversal of positions nor a powerless parody of power. It is a refutation in action of learned protest techniques and other demands. The weariness of traditional activist circles is left behind, and already a new horizon of joyful and creative acts is emerging.




The high school students’ strategic skill lies in reusing codes deemed harmless and far too childish to be repressed or even considered: superheroes, costumes, TikTok trends, and so on. Yet, each time, they repurpose these codes in a context of assault and offensives, leading to physical or non-physical confrontations with law enforcement. For example, Captain America launches an attack followed by hundreds of individuals dressed in black. These actions further expose the fundamental illegitimacy of police officers using force. And besides, what can a police officer do against a Batman who starts dancing in front of him? Get enraged, strike, or experience boredom, or endure his docility (the latter two obligations usually being reserved for high school students). How do you stop a battle of auras, the apotheosis of absurdity and humour? By no other means than as a spoilsport. One last thing: what can a police officer do when faced with a left-wing activist, some kind of proselytizer, megaphone in hand, shouting the same old slogans? Ignore them like any other piece of scenery.




Rediscovered Lucidity(ies)




One of the obvious attributes of the complicity present before and during October 17th (Gen Z, students, temporary workers, suburbanites, subordinates, Yellow Vests—in short, subjectivities in the process of proletarianisation) is their propensity for the “playful”. The innocuous act of triggering an aura battle, like smashing a shop window, even if they share no fundamental equivalence, manifests this same playful relationship to the metropolitan imposition of a commercial space. It would be wrong to oppose acts of rage and destruction to the expression of newfound joy, or in other words, acts of looting and arson to role-playing, aura battles, and dressing up as superheroes. They condense and stem from the same affects: in short, a joy in destruction or the anticipation of destroying with joy. Against the contained, regular, and monotonous movements and displacements of the urban and commercial world, always assigned to a goal, they also oppose and demonstrate the here and now possibility of free activity, of a reclaiming of space, without a stated goal or pre-established function. In 

Homo Ludens

, Johan Huizinga defines play as follows:




Summing up the formal characteristics of play we might call it a free activity standing quite consciously outside “ordinary” life as being “not serious”, but at the same time absorbing the player intensely and utterly. )t is an activity connected with no material interest, and no profit can be gained by it. It proceeds within its own proper boundaries of time and space according to fixed rules and in an orderly manner. It promotes the formation of social groupings which tend to surround themselves with secrecy and to stress their difference from the common world by disguise or other means

.

[2]




Material appropriation through the destruction of property or self-reduction, and amusement in its various forms of staging, are found within the realm of play. Ultimately, there is nothing surprising about this return of play if we understand it and situate it within the long decline of the school system, which has relentlessly sought to ward off all possible manifestations of play and the reappropriation of daily life: distractions, amusement, subversion, and even, until recently, the use of the telephone. Playfulness must be distinguished from the petit-bourgeois conception of fighting as festive folklore, with its infamous techno dances, the vanguard of militant harmlessness.




In front of high schools and elsewhere, these acts serve to expose adult seriousness and its posturing of exemplary behavior, the last vestiges of a still-latent complicity with repressive educational institutions (how many outraged and revealing reactions were provoked by the burning of the Nelson Mandela Secondary School in Nantes?). Suspending boredom, escaping the rigid, academic environment, learning skills independent of their commercial and professional applications, refusing to succumb to resignation and inaction in the face of catastrophe—these are the areas in which play offers an option.




But why claim that this playful quality can shed light on last Saturday’s astonishing and powerful offensive? Does not a better analysis require discerning, within the material circumstances, what underlay the movement? Surely.




Often, the desire to explain the causes of an insurrectionary process contains a prescriptive intent. The aim is to better understand it and make its continuation even more efficient. The effort is commendable. But it often amounts to saying what happened in order to better explain what should happen next. As Walter Benjamin pointed out in his time: “The destructive character has no interest in being understood.”

[3]

 The efforts made in this direction seem superficial to it. Being understood is a bourgeois affair. The destroyer, for its part, does not care. It does not want disciples. It prefers to be alone, for it is the only way for it to bear witness to the solitude of what is destroyed. The incomprehension provoked by looting must sometimes be accompanied by a refusal of any time-consuming explanation, any attempt to make oneself respectable. Nevertheless, considering this activity as minimally “playful,” that breaking a shop window, breaking into stores, sometimes stealing merchandise blindly and as quickly as possible, saying that it is an act of play, is often clearer than any imaginable justification. Learning from the effectiveness of October 17th must therefore be done without trying to deduce, fix, or project desirable forms of future insurrection. Otherwise, the risk is that the event will be reincorporated into a militant body of manners, gestures, and knowledge that is profoundly antithetical and impotent.




Against Vigilance




The audacious act of October 17th stemmed in part from a combination of playful exuberance and a rejection of the usual anxieties about “consequences”. Indeed, the high school students’ offensive also lay in its ability to bypass the vigilance reflexes of informed, autonomous activists. The acts were regularly carried out openly, broadcast live, and sometimes the rioters even posed proudly with their “trophies.”




Some comrades noticed this and appreciated it, while others, more numerous, and based on the series of convictions, deplored it. We are not advocating blindly attacking shop windows without considering the extent of the surveillance and resources mobilised afterward; or, more simply and foolishly, encouraging everyone to rush headlong into the fray. But within this playful unleashing of looting, there is a kind of impulsive, reckless impulse that comes first, an unconsciousness that ultimately reflects what this struggle represents: an existential stake, a life force expressed in a “whatever-it-takes-it” and a “regardless-of-the-repercussions” attitude. Far from establishing a politics of rioting or providing a perfect tool for understanding, this “recklessness” allows us to shift our traditional conceptions of commitment, so often linked to the fear of repression. Rather than conceiving of the struggle as a rational calculation of contingencies and risks (“how to risk less and do more?”), the riotous act refuses to be confined to this accounting logic. We must act here and now, rediscover a 

kairos

 compatible with collective desire, before even considering anticipating the worst and, consequently, relegating revolutionary action to a fictitious future detached from our time. Because what the spread of anti-repression practices as a whole carries with it, however welcome they may always be, is a desire for post-insurrection stabilisation, a yearning to present a serene and comprehensible model of revolt. Yet, by its very nature, the continuation of revolt is a leap into the utter unknown, a novelty with which we must strive to come to terms.




Moreover, while prisons and endless trials may frighten us, the existence that awaits us is remarkably similar. In these circumstances, rediscovering playfulness can also mean, like 

Ritchy Thibault

 and his irreverent public hearings, refusing to bow to the legal charade and its deceptive games.




Maintaining this playful irresponsibility short-circuits the deterrent power of the pervasive security rhetoric, characterised by a continuous dissemination of new measures, tools, and sophisticated repressive forces: the use of AI, 

DNA guns

, liquids that permanently soak into clothing, the deployment of the 

RAID

, the 

GIGN

, the Army… There is no need to elaborate on the arsenal at the state’s disposal for counter-insurgency. High school students and Gen Z, the new professional conspirators in chief, are showing us the way to neutralise them; to ward off risk, to embrace irresponsibility.







[1]

 A traditional French children’s nursery rhyme and staring game known as “Le jeu de la barbichette” (

Wikipedia

)

.




[2]

 Johan Huizinga, 

Homo Ludens: A Study of the Play-Element in Culture

 [1938], Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1949, p. 13.




[3]

 Walter Benjamin, “The Destructive Character”, originally published in the 

Frankfurter Zeitung

, November 20th 1931 (

The Anarchist Library

).

title: Open letter from the prisoners of October 17, 2026
content:
from 

lundimatin

 #539, 28/10/2026







For weeks, the repression against the ongoing movement has intensified. In the aftermath of October 17th, Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin, flouting all separation of powers, ordered the judiciary to hand down the harshest possible sentences to arrested and prosecuted protesters. Many of them are now in prison. Some of the prisoners from October 17th managed to send us this open letter, which serves as both a confession and a call to continue the struggle.




We are writing to you from a prison in the Île-de-France region, the name of which we will not disclose, in order to protect ourselves from the risk of reprisals and, above all, from the judicial and prison authorities.







We are students, high school students, teachers, the unemployed, restaurant owners, small business owners, delivery drivers, gangsters, from every neighborhood and every city in the region: Créteil, Bobigny, Belleville, Montreuil, Bagnolet, Noisy-le-Sec, Seine-et-Marne, Seine-Saint-Denis, and Paris. We are of all ages, all skin colors, and all nationalities; we are Arabs, Whites, Blacks, Roma, Turks, Germans, and French.




We have been accused, rightly or wrongly, of looting, of committing violence against law enforcement, of assembling illegally, of concealing our faces. Ultimately, our situations and the accusations against us are irrelevant, because the courts have bowed to Macron’s orders and sent us all to jail. Even though each prison is all the more the unsanitary and overcrowded as a consequence, next, as long as they fit!




This reminds us how what we call Justice is in no way an independent institution, especially when the State and the bourgeoisie feel threatened.




In prison, we have the privilege of being able to numb ourselves all day in front of BFMTV, CNEWS, and the channels of the regime’s other watchdogs. The ideological offensive on these TV stations supports the repressive policies of those who think they govern us. This offensive is commensurate with the fear that has gripped them since last Saturday. It was a true revolutionary warning. Everywhere, they are now trying to make us regret it, to break us, to dissuade us from returning to future Saturdays. They are silencing the support, the pride, and all those little words we have read and heard in recent days, such as “I wish I had been there” or “you made them pay.” They want us to believe that our violence is comparable to the thousands of lives crushed by capitalism every day.




If the media mouthpieces of the powerful can’t define the “typical profile” of the insurgents, it’s because we are the people who have risen up. The people who suffer and who are now fighting to end their suffering. They try to divide us, to categorise us as protesters, vandals, looters, thugs, or far-left extremists. But they haven’t understood that we are all of these things at once! We are united by our anger and our desire for revolution. A revolution that gives us back the possibility to breathe and hope, to share and to work together. To finally allow us to decide how we want to live. A revolution that puts an end to this humiliation that oozes luxury.




This social rage drove us into the streets last Saturday; it’s the same rage that simmers in the corridors and cells of the prison where we are locked up. This rage also explains the support and respect other prisoners have for the October 17th uprising. Nor will we accept being separated into political prisoners and common criminals, because we were all driven into the prisons of this regime by this unjust world.




For all these reasons, we tell you emphatically, we regret nothing! Nothing except not having adequately protected ourselves against the repressive violence that was about to be unleashed upon us.




We therefore call on all those who are outside to continue standing up to the State and to return to the streets every Saturday, until the fall of Macron and his entire corrupt world.




We call on you to organise yourselves between each Saturday, to meet with one another, to prepare yourselves, and to take control of your lives now.




We call on you to support all prisoners like us and all uprisings, both here and elsewhere.




We urge you to avoid small shops as much as possible, to remind everyone that our people’s justice only targets the biggest, the richest, the multinationals—those who have been robbing, crushing, and despising us for far too long.




We urge you to reject any division among us and to loudly proclaim what we are fighting for: revolution.
